meta.title: Who really said "Laugh at what you hold sacred, and still hold it sacred"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: No source in Maslow's writings has been identified. Wikiquote files the line under "Attributed," citing a 1998 humour book published 28 years after his death.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Laugh at what you hold sacred, and still hold it sacred'?
meta.ogDescription: Credited to Abraham Maslow, but unsourced: the paper trail ends at a 1998 stress-and-humour book, not at anything Maslow wrote.

answer.label: Attributed to
answer.authorDates: 1908–1970 · American psychologist, founder of humanistic psychology
answer.sourceLine: Widely credited to Maslow, and squarely in keeping with his writing on self-actualizing people — his own list of their traits includes a “philosophical, unhostile sense of humor.” But no book, paper, lecture or journal entry of his has been shown to contain this sentence. Wikiquote files it under Attributed, and the only citation anyone offers is a 1998 stress-and-humour book published twenty-eight years after Maslow’s death.

source.heading: The paper trail

docMeta.dd: None located — absent from Maslow’s published books and papers

source.excerpt: Laugh at what you hold sacred, and still hold it sacred.
trail: Wikiquote’s Abraham Maslow page ↗ carries the line in its Attributed section, below the quotations it can tie to specific works, and gives one citation for it: Loretta LaRoche, p. xvii.
Open Library ↗ confirms that book — Relax — You May Only Have a Few Minutes Left: Using the Power of Humor to Overcome Stress in Your Life and Work, Loretta LaRoche, published by Villard in 1998.

Maslow died on 8 June 1970 ↗, so the only citation on offer post-dates him by twenty-eight years. Quote aggregators do not improve on it: A-Z Quotes ↗ lists the line and points back to the same 1998 book.

We searched the full text of Religions, Values, and Peak-Experiences — the Maslow book most concerned with the sacred, first published in 1964 ↗ — and the sentence does not appear in it. That is an absence, not a disproof, but it is where a line like this ought to have been.
source.excerptNote: There is no surrounding passage to quote. The sentence circulates as a free-standing aphorism, and every printed trail runs into a third party’s book rather than a page of Maslow’s.
source.rightsNote: Rights cannot be settled because the origin cannot be. No work by Maslow has been identified as containing this sentence, so there is no publication date to reason from — and nothing here should be treated as public domain. If the wording in fact originates with the 1998 LaRoche book rather than with Maslow, it would be in copyright to that author and publisher. Treat the line as of undetermined status and quote it with attribution and a hedge.

author.heading: Abraham Maslow
author.metaLine: 1908–1970 · American psychologist · Brandeis University · hierarchy of needs
author.bio: Abraham Maslow (born 1 April 1908, died 8 June 1970) was an American psychologist who spent most of his career at Brooklyn College and then Brandeis University, and who is remembered above all for the hierarchy of needs and the idea of self-actualization. His major books — Motivation and Personality (1954), Toward a Psychology of Being (1962) and Religions, Values, and Peak-Experiences (1964) — argued that psychology had studied sickness so thoroughly it had forgotten to study health. Humour genuinely mattered to him: in his portrait of self-actualizing people, a “philosophical, unhostile sense of humor” sits in the list alongside spontaneity, autonomy and peak experiences — which is exactly why a line like this one attaches to him so easily.

misattribution.heading: What’s actually wrong here
misattribution.intro: No rival author claims this sentence. The problem is not a wrong name — it is a missing source, quietly presented as though one existed.

items.why: Wikiquote ↗ puts the line in its Attributed list, separate from the quotations it can tie to Motivation and Personality (1954), The Psychology of Science (1966) and his other books. It is not filed as a fake — it is filed as unproven.

Even the big aggregators end up here: A-Z Quotes ↗ credits the line to Maslow but sources it to LaRoche’s Relax — You May Only Have a Few Minutes Left (1998) — A-Z Quotes and Wikiquote both print that title with the words transposed, as You May Have Only. A book about stress reduction quoting Maslow is not Maslow.

Maslow really did treat humour as a marker of psychological health — a “philosophical, unhostile sense of humor” is one of the traits he listed for self-actualizing people ↗. The line fits him so well that nobody thought to ask where it came from.

misattribution.truthLine: Honest verdict: attributed, not verified. Nothing shows the line is someone else’s, and nothing shows it is Maslow’s either — Wikiquote’s own filing ↗ is the most careful statement available, and it stops short of a source.

context.heading: Why this one sticks to Maslow
lead: The sentence does a neat trick in eleven words: it refuses the usual bargain in which reverence and comedy are enemies. That is a recognisably mid-century humanistic idea, and Maslow is the mid-century humanist most people can name — so the line lands on him the way stray wit lands on Mark Twain and stray uplift lands on Einstein.

There is also a real hook. When Maslow catalogued the characteristics of self-actualizing people, he did not treat humour as decoration; a philosophical, unhostile sense of humor is one of the listed traits, sitting beside spontaneity, autonomy and peak experiences. A quote that says you can mock a thing and still kneel to it sounds like something that catalogue could have produced. Sounding like an author is not the same as being written by one.
detailsBody: The paper trail is short and it runs the wrong way. Wikiquote’s entry cites the line to page xvii of Loretta LaRoche’s Relax — You May Only Have a Few Minutes Left, a humour-and-stress-reduction book published by Villard in 1998. Maslow died in June 1970. A citation twenty-eight years posthumous is not evidence of authorship; it is evidence that by 1998 the line was already circulating with his name on it.

That is the shape of a quotation that has slipped its moorings rather than one that was invented to deceive. It may yet turn out to be Maslow — from a lecture, a seminar, an unpublished journal page, or a paraphrase of him that hardened into a quotation. Until a page number in something he actually wrote turns up, the honest label is attributed, not said.
context.pull: The attribution is plausible, which is precisely why nobody ever checked it.

sourcesVerified.claim: Wikiquote lists "Laugh at what you hold sacred, and still hold it sacred." in its Attributed section, citing Loretta LaRoche, Relax — You May Have Only a Few Minutes Left (1998), p. xvii — not among the sourced quotations from Maslow's own books.

Abraham Maslow was an American psychologist, born 1 April 1908 and died 8 June 1970, who taught at Brooklyn College and Brandeis, and published Motivation and Personality (1954), Toward a Psychology of Being (1962), Religions, Values, and Peak-Experiences (1964) and The Farther Reaches of Human Nature (1971).
Loretta LaRoche's Relax - You May Only Have a Few Minutes Left: Using the Power of Humor to Overcome Stress in Your Life and Work was published in 1998 by Villard.
A-Z Quotes lists "Laugh at what you hold sacred, and still hold it sacred" credited to Abraham Maslow and sources it to Loretta LaRoche's 1998 book, not to any work by Maslow.
Maslow's list of characteristics of self-actualizing people includes "Philosophical, unhostile sense of humor" (item 13 of 14).

Complete text of Maslow's Religions, Values, and Peak-Experiences (1964 Kappa Delta Pi / 1970 Viking preface, Penguin edition), including all nine appendices — downloaded and searched; the words "laugh"/"sacred" never occur together and the sentence does not appear anywhere in it.
Internet Archive holds Maslow's Religions, Values, and Peak-Experiences, Ohio State University Press, 1964.
Internet Archive holds Maslow's Motivation and Personality, Harper, New York, 1954.
Checked as an anchor source: Quote Investigator has no article investigating this quote — a site-restricted search for the phrase returns no QI page on it.
